title: I contain multitudes
hookLine: do I contradict myself? very well then, I contradict myself (Song of Myself 51)
tomorrow: why did Whitman walk out of the astronomy lecture?

cards: Someone digs up your old posts to prove you used to think the opposite. Near the end of Song of Myself, Whitman sees that coming and gets there first.
"Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)" No apology. Just a shrug the size of a continent.
And he lived it: he kept reworking Leaves of Grass, edition after edition, so the book itself kept changing.

teach.b: Readers who love him split on this line. One side hears an escape hatch. Say anything, and when someone catches you, announce that you're large.
Integrity, they'd say, means your words and your life line up over time, and it's why promises mean something. That view has teeth.

teach.h: THE OTHER: A SELF BIG ENOUGH.
teach.b: The other side hears the center of his whole teaching. For Whitman the self isn't a small fixed point.
It's big enough to hold old and young, body and soul, doubt and faith, and he refuses to cut off half of himself to look neat.
Emerson had put the same thought sharply in his essay Self-Reliance: "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds." Notice the word foolish.
Not every consistency: the foolish kind, the kind that keeps you saying yesterday's sentence after you've outgrown it. Both sides can agree on that much. Whitman isn't saying anything goes.
He's saying a living person is bigger than the last thing they said.
So that's the teaching: I contain multitudes. Not a license to break your word, but permission to stop pretending you're only one thing.

how: Some readers of Whitman quote section 51 of Song of Myself when someone is caught between two true things about themselves; some keep the line written somewhere they'll see it.

games.why: that's the strongest form of the worry. Whitman's side answers: not every consistency, only the foolish kind; a living self is larger than its last sentence.

practice: Sit up and rest one hand on each knee. Let the right hand hold one thing that's true of you, and the left its opposite: brave and scared, wanting home and wanting away. Breathe, and leave both hands where they are.

wordCard.voice: I contain multitudes: Whitman's answer to his own contradictions. A self large enough to hold its opposites, without pretending to be only one thing.

carryVoice: Carry this: I contain multitudes. Room for both hands, and for the person you're still becoming. See you tomorrow.
